segments.text: **Speech: 4**

**Hon. Kalaignar M. Karunanidhi:** Hon. Speaker, yesterday and today, members and leaders belonging to all parties have brought together and presented their views on the Industries grant and have told this Government the ways in which the industrial sector in Tamil Nadu can be developed further. I convey my thanks to all of them. From Subramanian, who began speaking yesterday on behalf of the Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, up to Kumari Ananthan, Deputy Leader of our Congress party, everyone who spoke has offered many constructive views on the development of industry in Tamil Nadu. Our friend Ugamchand alone kept looking around for some way or other to find fault with this Government and remained engaged in that effort until the end of his speech. I neither prevent nor condemn the effort he has taken to criticise this Government somehow; on the contrary, if even in that there are ways by which this Government should correct itself, I will accept them too, and I give the assurance that this Government will strive and work accordingly for industrial development.
Yesterday, our friend Poovaragan, while speaking, said that the amount allotted for this industrial development was very small.

He calculated only the amounts allotted under these two demands. Under Demand No. 24, Industries, Rs. 6.53 crore has been allotted, and under Demand No. 51, Capital Expenditure on Industrial Development, Rs. 22.24 crore; calculating only these, he regretted that it was merely Rs. 28 crore. But if the Rs. 19 crore under Demand No. 59, Loans and Advances by the State Government, which is not under discussion now, is added, it comes to Rs. 47.77 crore. Not only that. Arrangements have also been made to borrow Rs. 4.37 crore in the open market with a Government guarantee. Adding this too, I am duty-bound to state that the total allocation for 1990-91 is Rs. 52.14 crore. Compared with 1989-90, when the amount allotted in that year's Budget was Rs. 44.29 crore, I am duty-bound to point out that it has now risen to Rs. 52.14 crore. The Hon. members of this House know very well that, rather than the State Government directly putting capital into industries, it is far more concerned with encouraging industries.

Therefore, even though the allocation made directly by the Government is of this order, if the amounts and capital made available through other financial institutions and banks and Government industrial undertakings, including equity, are all taken together, one can see that the allocation available for industry in our State is substantial. I spoke in this grant last year about this Government's industrial policy. I am duty-bound to remind the House of it again today.

Yesterday, our friend Ponnusamy, while speaking, placed before the House certain reports suggesting that we are today ruining all private industry, driving private entrepreneurs away, and that they are afraid even to start industries. Though I denied that allegation even then, as far as this Government is concerned, alongside the existing “Joint Sector,” last year we created another category called the “Associate Sector” and announced that such industries would be undertaken as joint ventures with the private sector, with the Government holding 20 per cent in the Joint Sector and 11 per cent in the Associate Sector. We have also already announced a scheme under which even these higher Government shareholdings may, at the appropriate time, be realised through “disinvestment” and the amount used for new industries.

Therefore, if 26 per cent is said to be the Government's share, nobody should imagine that “Government” is something situated somewhere apart from the people. The Government's 26 per cent is the people's share. Twenty-six per cent is the Government share; 25 per cent is the private sector's share; all the remaining percentage consists of the public's shares, their share capital. Thus the public's share capital and the Government's share capital are both, in essence, the people's share capital. Even if we separately call it “Government,” it is the people's share. In a situation where the people's share is so large, this Government will certainly not tolerate private parties who, without even holding the appropriate share capital and with a share smaller than that, nevertheless seek to exercise complete domination over an industry. That is why, for several years, in one company to which they referred—

when a situation arose in which a member of that family was Chairman, another member of that family was the M.D., and the son of a member of that family was also in the company, we acquired the duty to point this out to them.

The Central Government itself made an announcement in 1976. In that year it expressed the view that, in joint-sector undertakings, the Chairman should be appointed on behalf of the Government. It is on that basis, and because a situation should not exist in which large amounts belonging to the Government are being used while the Government has no representation whatsoever, that we have now initiated action. Private companies need not fear merely because this problem has arisen in one company; but any private company that follows the same practice should also know that the Government will not hesitate to act. I am greatly duty-bound to state that this is the Government's definite policy in the industrial sector.

Those who spoke yesterday said: you have been in office for fifteen months; how many factories have you seen? Factories are not things that can be established by magical tricks, with a foundation stone laid today and production beginning tomorrow. For a factory to be established, studies, arrangements and investments all have to take place.
In that connection, I stated last year that, even in the case of factories announced by the previous Government before this Government came into being but left standing without any action—

we did not abandon them merely because the previous Government had announced them. This Government took steps to start all those factories and implemented efforts involving expenditure of Rs. 62.3 crore. To give the details: Tamil Nadu Magnesium and Marine Chemicals at Valinokkam, a factory undertaken by TIDCO alone at a cost of Rs. 9.60 crore. This factory produces magnesium metal from waste brine. This metal is used in atomic-power production. Production has already begun there. This was announced by the previous Government, but no action had been taken and it had lain dormant; I wish to state that it has now begun production.

Next, Titan Watches. The watch-making industry had already been started at Hosur. A Cases and Precisions project, costing about Rs. 30 crore, has been established in the SIPCOT industrial complex at Hosur, with TIDCO and the Tata company jointly manufacturing watches in the joint sector. I am happy to state here that the watches produced in this factory are today the most widely sold in India. Until now the cases required for those watches had been imported from abroad; to change that situation and make them there itself, the factory has been expanded this year to the extent of about Rs. 30 crore.

Sakthi Soyas Limited is a joint-sector undertaking. TIDCO and Sakthi have jointly established it near Pollachi with a capital of Rs. 22.48 crore. It is a factory producing cooking oil from soya. Production—
has also commenced, I wish to state.

I would further like to give details of industries that will begin production this year. U.P. Petro Products Limited is a joint-sector factory being started at Manali with a capital of Rs. 80.65 crore. All construction work is nearing completion. The work of installing machinery will be completed in another two months. It is a factory producing polyols and other petroleum products. Polyols are a material useful for plastics industries and some other industries.

Fifth is Tamil Nadu Telecommunications Limited, a factory in a joint venture of the Central and State Governments producing telephone cables and certain equipment required for telephones. It is located at Arakkonam at a cost of Rs. 23.30 crore. The State Government has a 25 per cent share and the Central Government 26 per cent. Construction work began in May 1989, and the work is progressing rapidly enough for the machinery to arrive by July 1990 and operations to begin.

Sixth is Sangam Aluminium Limited. This is a joint-sector factory being started at Denkanikottai with an investment of Rs. 10.35 crore. Aluminium products will be manufactured there. Construction work is in progress. Machinery will be installed in September and production is to begin in December.

Seventh, Integrated Waterproofing Limited, at a cost of Rs. 4.62 crore, has been started in the joint sector at Alamathi village in Chengai-Anna district, and all construction work has begun. The machinery has been imported. The factory will begin functioning soon.

Eighth, North Arcot Leathers Limited, is a tannery started at Kalanipakkam near Vaniyambadi at a cost of Rs. 1.60 crore. Construction work is proceeding rapidly. This too is a joint-sector undertaking.

Next, if we take factories where work has begun but is not yet complete: ninth, “Dyna Lamps and Glass Works,” a factory to be started near Gummidipoondi at a cost of Rs. 42.70 crore in the joint sector by TIDCO and Dynavision. Equipment required for electric lamps will be manufactured there. Approval has been given for an IDBI loan. The work will begin shortly.

Tenth, Reliance Ceramics at Madurantakam, a joint-sector factory costing Rs. 20.40 crore, in which TIDCO, Light Roofings and Reliance Ceramic companies are joining to manufacture polished floor and wall tiles. An IDBI loan has been obtained for it. It will begin production this year.

Eleventh, Ushtade Biotex Industries, at Cuddalore, is a joint-sector factory with capital of Rs. 20 crore for producing artificial sweetener, run jointly by TIDCO and a Calcutta-based company called Ushtade. Construction work is under way. Only recently I attended its foundation-stone function.

Among the works announced and factories now in progress after the Kazhagam Government returned to office, twelfth is Pil Co Glass Company Limited, a joint-sector factory to be started at Bhuvanagiri at a cost of Rs. 17.90 crore. Land was acquired, the foundation-stone function was held on 27-8-1989, and work is in progress. Sheet glass is to be manufactured there.

Thirteenth is Dandeck Agro Chemicals Limited, a pesticide factory to be established in the joint sector at Cuddalore at a cost of Rs. 5.48 crore. Its foundation stone too was laid on 27-8-1989 and work is in progress.

Fourteenth, Sterling Dungston Products, is a joint-sector factory being started at Cuddalore at a cost of Rs. 45 crore. Tungsten powder is a product of great use to the defence sector. Talks for a technical agreement with a Korean company are proceeding rapidly. The factory, with an investment of Rs. 45 crore, is expected to start soon.
Apart from these, approval has recently been given to three more projects—large industrial projects.

The Aniline project is a joint-sector factory at Ranipet with an expenditure of Rs. 110 crore to manufacture chemicals such as aniline, nitric acid and ammonium nitrate. I also wish to state that some machinery for this factory has already been imported.

Sixteenth is a “Mineral Separation Plant,” an industry with an investment of Rs. 20 crore to be jointly run by the Central and State Governments. It will be located at Kuthiraimozhitheri in Chidambaranar district. Products such as thorium and illuminite will be produced there.
An agreement for this has been entered into with Indian Rare Earth, a Central Government undertaking.
Seventeenth is a titanium-di-oxide factory, to be started in the joint sector at the same Kuthiraimozhitheri at a cost of Rs. 140 crore.

Thus, in answer to the question whether fifteen factories had come in fifteen months, I have placed before this House a list of seventeen factories: factories that had been announced but were not implemented, factories announced and immediately started, factories beginning production this year, and factories whose production may begin next year but whose construction and machinery-import work will be completed this year.

Next, Hon. member Mani and others who spoke here stressed that we must secure for Tamil Nadu many factories for which Central Government permission is required and in which the Central Government invests. They stressed the need to secure many Central-investment factories for Tamil Nadu. I wish to state that this Government has not been sluggish in that matter either.

Even while speaking, the Deputy Leader of our Congress party expressed the view that an oil refinery should be established in Tamil Nadu, particularly in the Nagai area. The leaders and members of the parties who spoke yesterday and today have described the possibilities for industries to spring up and flourish in different parts of Tamil Nadu and throughout the State. We—

have not remained unconcerned, weary, negligent or indifferent about obtaining Central Government assistance or permission for industries that require such assistance or permission. I am duty-bound to point that out.

The Madras Refineries company and Southern Petrochemicals company have jointly formed “NATCO.” With a project at Manali costing Rs. 1,356 crore for the manufacture of petrochemical products, the Government has already undertaken steps to acquire the required land. We are continuing to discuss it with the Central Government in person and to write to them. Recently, in a letter I wrote to the Prime Minister of India on 2-4-1990 regarding the factory to be established by the National Aromatics and Petrochemicals Corporation, I wrote: “While the feasibility report was submitted in July 1989, the capacity of the project was enhanced to 2 lakhs tonnes of P.P.A. as per Government Policy, and the report was revised with a total investment cost of Rs. 1,356 Crores in September 1989. Environmental Clearances both from State and Central Governments have been obtained and the project is pending before the P.I.B. for clearance”; and, seeking immediate approval, I further wrote: “As the project does not depend on the Government of India for financed and as it is, a major venture in our State after more than a decade, I would be grateful, if you could use your good offices for the early clearance of the said project by the P.I.B. and others, without further postponement which would only result in avoidable cost escalation. . . . .” I have received a reply from the Prime Minister stating that it would be attended to immediately.

Likewise, the Deputy Leader of the Congress party referred here to gas. Yesterday our Vellingiri also referred to it. None of the members who spoke here failed to mention it. They spoke about the benefits of gas and the efforts we should make to obtain it. In order to facilitate the establishment in Tamil Nadu of factories manufacturing various petrochemical products, we had already asked for a gas connection for the South during Rajiv Gandhi's period in office. When the Minister concerned came here for a function and I participated in it, I raised the matter and he said, “It is a good idea; we will examine it.” Subsequently, after that Government changed and the National Front Government came to office, we reminded them again. I met Mr Gurupadaswamy in Delhi and spoke to him, and later, when he came to Chennai and met me, I pressed the matter. On that basis, in a letter dated 6-4-1990, he wrote to me: “Please refer to your D.O. letter, dated 22-2-1990 regarding the laying of a Southern Gas pipeline from Bombay High. I am glad to inform you that we have decided to constitute and Inter-Ministerial Committee to examine the issues pertaining to the construction of Southern Gas Grid. We are anxious that the available gas is utilised as quickly as possible. This matter would therefore continue to receive our highest priority.” They sent this reply promptly. I appreciate that reply. On behalf of this House, I ask the Central Ministers to continue the efforts promptly and take the necessary steps so that our demands are fulfilled.

Everyone here has also asked about the Salem steel plant. This morning our Mr Ramani spoke here. Mr Pandian spoke here. The Deputy Leader of our Congress party spoke. Everyone has spoken about it. This Government is continuously arguing for the Salem steel-plant project. A false campaign is being conducted in some publications today saying that this Government has not argued for the project. Nobody can forget that it was the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam Government that argued and struggled for a steel plant at Salem and succeeded, as early as 1971. But the Salem steel plant approved then did not take shape in the manner we had envisaged; it became something else. That is why, even now, I referred to it in a letter I wrote to the Hon. Prime Minister of India, Mr V.P. Singh:
“Dear Prime Minister,

On the basis of the representation made by me to the late Thirumathi Indira Gandhi, the Salem Steel Plant was approved in 1970. Accordingly in original detailed project report it envisaged the manufacture of stainless steel, cilicon steel and special steel and installation of hot rolling and cold rolling facilities. However only a cold rolling complex for the production of 32,000 tonnes of stainlees steel sheet were commissioned in 1981 in the first stage. The original conception of an integrated steel plant has thus been grossly diluted and what has been installed in Salem is largely in the nature of a Stainless Steel Rolling Mill. Our Government has been representing from time for the setting up hot rolling facilities to enable the upstream integration of this plant. We are aware that considerable investment is taking place in North India in

regard to modernistion of steel plant and a case for further investment in the existing facilities in Salem in order to realize the original conception should not be delayed any further. The Durgapur Steel Plant has been modified at a considerable cost to make stainless steel continuous cast slabs which are now being sent all the way to Finland for rolling into hot roll coil. With the setting up of hot rolling facilities at Salem, there is scope for considerable saving of foreign exchange. The project will provide direct employment to 2500 persons and will also generate considerable indirect employment in the ancilary and tertiary sectors. I will be grateful if you can give this your sympathetic consideration and have the project included in the Eighth Plan. On our part we shall take all steps to meet the additional power requirement for the project once the detailed time-schedule is worked out.”

The Prime Minister sent the letter I had written to the Minister of the department and discussed it with him. The Minister, Mr Dinesh Goswami, then wrote to me: “Please refer to your letter of January 22, 1990 in regard to the establishment of hot rolling facilities at Salem Steel Plant. I appreciate and share your concern in the matter. The growth of Salem Steel Plant has been engaging the attention of the Government. While the work of doubling the capacity of the Plant by installation of a second Spensioner Mill is currently in progress, the question of installing hot rolling facilities at Salem as well as the proposal to include it in the Eighth Plan are also under the active consideration of the Government. We shall keep in mind your concern in coming to a final decision.”

Likewise, regarding expansion of the Manali fertiliser factory, I wrote to the Central Government, to the Agriculture Minister and to Deputy Prime Minister Mr Devi Lal. In his reply dated 10-4-1990 he wrote: “Please refer to your letter, dated 22nd February, 1990 regarding the Schemes of Madras Fertilisers Limited. As regards the expansion of the

existing Fertilisers Plant of M.F.L., the Company was advised to prepare a detailed project report for its revamping modernisation and also for its replacement by a new Plant. In this context a detailed project report for revamping modernisation of the existing plant of M.F.L. has been received. It contains two alternatives. While the first alternative is intended to prolong the life of the existing plant at an investment of Rs.105 crores approximately, the second alternative involving an expenditure of about Rs. 240 crores will improve the existing capacity and production. Both the alternatives are being examined. Devi Lal -” That is the letter he wrote.

I have taken all this trouble, at this advanced age, for Tamil Nadu's industrial prosperity—not being young like our Rajendran, as he himself said—in order to demonstrate that we are continuously pursuing efforts with the Central Government, both directly and through correspondence, to secure Central Government permission for major industries here and to have many industries established here with Central capital.

Likewise, in the policy note I have mentioned an effort to establish in South Arcot district a project using bagasse to manufacture annually one lakh metric tonnes of artificial paper and one lakh metric tonnes of writing paper. I wish to speak about it now too. Our friend Mr Ugamchand asked: when a factory was then to be set up for Rs. 240 crore, was it really so much, and is it now Rs. 800 crore? We should not forget that ten years have rolled by in between. If we consider how much even the salaries of our MLAs have increased, we can understand the extent to which inflation has affected us. (Interruption.) Laughter.
That can be left to the Leader of the House during the Assembly debate. (Laughter.)

Therefore, it is because cost estimates have today risen tenfold and twentyfold that, if a factory could then have been established for Rs. 240 or Rs. 250 crore, it now requires Rs. 800 crore. We have not yet determined in which part or at which location in South Arcot district this factory will be established. The necessary studies are in progress. We are also pursuing the matter with the Central Government. I therefore state in this House that South Arcot district needs a major paper factory and that we will make rapid efforts to establish it in that district within a year or two.

Sugar factories were discussed here. Our Ilakkiya Selvar also said that because you have kept it in the cooperative sector—“cooperative sector”—private parties are going to other States. I consider that Tamil Nadu already has an adequate number of sugar mills. Even if one or two private mills go elsewhere, there are enough sugar mills here in the public, private and cooperative sectors for us not to be worried. There are at present 29 sugar mills in all: 14 in the private sector, 12 in the cooperative sector and 3 in the public sector. Under the Seventh Five-Year Plan, permission was granted and a decision taken to establish nine mills—five private mills and four cooperative mills. Among the five private mills are Sakthi Sugar Mill, Sivaganga, Dharani Sugar Mill, Vasudevanallur—the one mentioned just now when somebody said that we are driving away “N.R.I.” persons—

that Dharani Sugar Mill is the mill run by Periyasamy. If it is run properly, we will not interfere; if it is run improperly, this is an example showing that this Government will not hesitate to intervene. I also wish to point out that private mills such as Periyakulam Rajshree Sugar Mill, Thiruvaruran Sugar Mill and Poondi Sugar Mill have received permission but have not yet started.

Likewise, four cooperative sugar mills: one at Sethiyathope in Chidambaram has been started under the name M.R. Krishnamurthy Cooperative Sugar Mill. In a few days, on May 13, I am to attend the foundation-stone function for the Harur Cooperative Sugar Mill. All agreements for it have been completed and it has today reached the stage where the mill can be started. The Cheyyar Cooperative Sugar Mill will start in November 1990. Questions were raised about the Aranthangi Cooperative Sugar Mill. Since water is a major problem there, studies are being conducted. I also wish to state that the State Government has recommended to the Central Government the establishment of cooperative sugar mills in taluks such as Ambasamudram, Chinna Salem, Polur and Gummidipoondi.

Next, many members spoke here about electricity generation. The Deputy Leader of the Congress party spoke at length. Since a financial statement or report relating to the Electricity Department will certainly be placed before this House this year and is to be debated, we can discuss it in detail then. Even so, Hon. member Professor Ponnusamy made an accusation the other day that the amount we have allotted for electricity is much lower than in previous years.

In 1987-88, the plan allocation for electricity was Rs. 407.63 crore, but the amount actually spent was only Rs. 372.29 crore. In 1988-89, the annual plan of the Government then in office was announced as Rs. 1,457 crore, and within that announcement Rs. 502 crore was said to be for electricity. But because the Rs. 1,457 crore plan itself shrank to Rs. 1,202 crore, the Rs. 502 crore electricity allocation too shrank to Rs. 352.53 crore. Compared with that Rs. 352 crore, the truth is clear that our allocation of Rs. 457 crore for electricity in 1990-91 is higher.

Not only that, we are taking steps to add another 287 MW of generation in 1990-91. Last year, 1989-90, 235 MW was added through Tamil Nadu Electricity Board schemes and 118 MW through schemes implemented by the Central Government, increasing capacity by a total of 353 MW. In 1988-89, electricity generated and received from other stations together amounted to only 17,585 million units. In 1989-90, despite many difficulties, we raised it to 18,672 million units. In 1990-91 we expect it to reach 21,089 million units. Under the Eighth Five-Year Plan, schemes have been initiated to create about 300 MW of additional generating capacity each year.

All members of the House know very well that the North Chennai power station was announced but could not be started because of a site dispute. That project was originally to be started at a cost of Rs. 500 crore. Only after this Government came to office was that site dispute resolved; now, at a cost of Rs. 700 crore, this project is being started—

and all of you know very well that the President came to inaugurate it after this Government created a favourable situation for the project. Work on the first two units, with a total capacity of 420 MW, is now set to proceed rapidly. Assistance from the Asian Development Bank has also been sought for a third unit of 210 MW. I am happy to state that this power station will ultimately have a generating capacity of 2,050 MW. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

Next, our Hon. members have spoken about TAMIN, granite and the wrongdoings that occurred there. I explained the matter in detail last year; therefore I wish to speak only briefly now. Hon. member Mr P.H. Pandian in particular asked why that officer has still been left in place. We must consider how the wrongdoing occurred. Hon. member Mr Vellingiri said, while speaking, that the profit earned this year had not come from production but from raising prices. There is some truth in that. Yes, we raised prices. How? Prices had deliberately been kept low. The Government undertaking, the public undertaking, TAMIN, sold at prices lower than those obtained by private parties, and because corruption took place as a result, and because an officer was responsible for it at that time, the undertaking suffered a major loss. Those prices were reviewed and action was taken during Governor's rule. It was only in November during Governor's rule that the true face of that officer became apparent. As soon as it became known in November, action was taken under Governor's rule. What happened was that, in 1983-84—

for a cubic metre of the two kinds of stone sold for export there—grey-coloured rock and black-coloured rock—the price fixed by TAMIN for grey stone was between 277 and 294 dollars, while private parties received 420 dollars for the same stone at the same time. In 1984-85 TAMIN received 258 to 269 dollars and private parties 475 dollars. In 1985-86 TAMIN received 299 dollars and private parties 460 dollars. In 1986-87 TAMIN received 404 to 427 dollars and private parties 475 dollars. In 1987-88 TAMIN received 512 to 538 dollars and private parties 575 dollars. It was then that the matter came to the Governor's attention and that officer was caught.

Not only that: the grey stone exported by TAMIN was of very good quality, while the grey stone exported by private parties was of much lower quality. Since the lower-quality private stone was sold at higher prices while TAMIN's better-quality stone was sold at lower prices, the undertaking suffered a major loss because of this corruption. In the case of black stone in 1986-87, look at the magnitude of the injustice: per cubic metre, TAMIN received 714 dollars and private parties 1,500 dollars. While private parties sold that lower-quality black stone for 1,500 dollars, our TAMIN sold at 714 dollars. The loss in one quarry alone because of this was Rs. 48 lakh.

In 1986, the Japanese company “Orient Sanyo” offered 1,281 dollars for the stone from the quarry at Thiruvakkarai. It came forward to pay 1,281 dollars per cubic metre. But TAMIN refused to supply it to them and instead exported to Mitsubishi Corporation at 550 dollars per cubic metre, the same price at which it had supplied in 1982. The loss in that one quarry alone was Rs. 41 lakh. During Governor's rule the old Managing Director—the Managing Director referred to by Pandian—was replaced. As soon as a new Managing Director was appointed, the November price of 714 dollars was changed and from December it began to be sold at 2,050 dollars per cubic metre—
a situation I am duty-bound to remind the House of.

This was the loss TAMIN suffered because of such price differences. TAMIN has more than about 3,500 acres of land; the loss arising from 2,500 acres at that time was Rs. 10 crore. That is why we are now taking action against that officer. The enquiry is proceeding in the proper manner. Because further action requires certain evidence, and because evidence is needed not only from here but also from abroad, there is some delay; but I state firmly that those who committed wrongdoing will certainly not be allowed to escape and will be punished. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

The figures for 1987-88 make the matter clear. In 1987-88, sales were Rs. 11.75 crore and the total loss was Rs. 11 lakh. In 1988-89, sales were Rs. 10.63 crore and profit Rs. 2.12 crore; even in the book they have wrongly printed it as 2.1. In 1989-90, sales were Rs. 14.14 crore and profit Rs. 5.27 crore. In the book, this 5.27 has been wrongly printed as 2.12; I ask that it be read correctly. When sales of Rs. 11 crore produced a loss of Rs. 11 lakh, and sales of Rs. 14 crore now produce a profit of Rs. 5 crore, one can understand how great the wrongdoing had been. Therefore I again state that the Government will not hesitate to investigate the wrongs committed there and take action.

Sivaganga graphite was also discussed here. This same officer was involved there too. It was a project drawn up while that officer was there. In 1984, a graphite beneficiation plant containing 85 per cent carbon content—

was initially proposed at a cost of Rs. 3.4 crore. Later, on the view that graphite with 96 per cent carbon content would command good demand abroad, a factory was planned at a project cost of Rs. 27 crore with a 100 per cent export orientation. Starting with Rs. 3.4 crore, it was turned into a Rs. 27 crore proposal on the basis that a higher-content product could be made and made suitable for 100 per cent export.

Approval for the scheme was discussed at meetings of the Tamil Nadu Government's Project Appraisal Committee in August-September 1988. At that meeting, the Chief Secretary said that, since other technology existed in the world, details such as machinery and estimates could be sought from the Hambol Heavy plant company. The then Chairman of the undertaking stated that he did not have those supporting materials and information. He was subsequently changed; as I have already said, he was changed during Governor's rule.

After that, as our friends here have pointed out, only the work of quarrying the stone has been going on there. But the study report has still not arrived. It will take some time to obtain the necessary reports from the “Indian Bureau of Mines,” Pandian Graphites and the National Metallurgical Laboratory. They have now given an assurance in a letter received on 9-4-1990 that the report—the detailed project report—will be submitted by June 15. Fourteen thousand tonnes of graphite ore have been quarried there. Its value is said to be approximately Rs. 55 lakh. In order to prevent more graphite from being quarried and left outside where it may deteriorate, the quarrying work has been stopped. After the study report is fully examined, action—
will be taken and the graphite industry will be started there, I wish to state.

Our Rajendran spoke here about starting a soda factory at Vedaranyam in Thanjavur district. Our friend Alagarsamy also referred to it. It began in the election manifesto as soda ash and has now become smaller; Rajendran raised the doubt whether even this would come. I wish to tell him this. When this project was studied as a soda-ash project, the estimate was that it would cost Rs. 250 crore. Regarding running this project, they asked: why did you go to Tata; could you not go to “TAC”? When the matter was referred to Tuticorin Alkali and Chemicals, they said that soda-ash production in our country, that is, India, is at present very high. In 1989-90 alone, demand was 15.40 lakh tonnes, while production is now at the level of 15.496 lakh tonnes. Therefore, they said, instead of starting a soda-ash factory and then having difficulty selling its output, another industry could be started, and they put forward the idea of a caustic-soda factory project. Its cost was estimated at Rs. 60 crore.

The Government has also decided to establish a Marine Chemical Complex at a cost of Rs. 14 or 15 crore, using the salt available in that area. For preparation of a project report, permission has been given to the joint-sector company “TAC” to appoint Tata Consultancy. “TAC” has the technology for manufacturing soda ash—

but, because it does not have definite technical arrangements for this particular technology, it has itself sought their assistance and approached Tata Consultancy. The Tamil Nadu Electricity Board is prepared to supply even the 15 MW of power required to establish a caustic-soda plant in the Vedaranyam area. Since all these arrangements have been made, I give the assurance here that both these factories will certainly come up in the Vedaranyam area.

N.R.I.s were discussed. I indicated my position at the outset. With regard to N.R.I.s, our friend Ponnusamy said here that we had created many obstacles for Palani Periyasamy. He entered into an agreement with the previous Government to construct a hotel here. It was even spoken of as a Joint Sector project and was referred to as the “Pallava Hotel.” I will not say there was anything wrong in that. But what was wrong was this: a site was given to him and its value was stated to be Rs. 1 crore 75 lakh. That was the mistake. A site worth Rs. 40 crore was valued at only Rs. 1¾ crore, and even that Rs. 1¾ crore did not have to be paid by him because the Government, as a partner, was treated as contributing that amount. It was only because Government land should not simply pass away into somebody's hands that we decided that the Government itself should take it back. There is no personal hostility toward anybody. He is running a sugar mill; we have not improperly interfered with it. This is a justified intervention. Because a property worth Rs. 40 crore—

cannot be handed to one individual for only Rs. 1¾ crore, with the Government joining as a partner and without even receiving the money. It was because this new Government could not accept such a situation that action was taken, and for no other reason.

That does not mean that N.R.I. people have stopped coming here. Our Ilakkiya Selvar Kumari Ananthan also spoke about it. Our Ugamchand too spoke about it. Many people connected with N.R.I.s are running industries in Tamil Nadu.
Madras Hydraulic Hose Pipe Private Limited, approximately Rs. 3 crore, is run by Mr Viswanath, who is in Kenya.
Likewise, Minjur Shell Castik Private Limited is run here by Nadimuthu and M.S. Durai, Saudi Arabia.

Crescent Ceramic, John Sundararajan, U.S.A.; Breeze Hotel Private Limited, Messrs R. Sivaraman and Associate, Sri Lanka; Uma Wire Product Private Limited, Sadasan, Nigeria; Vasthira Appliance Private Limited, Nithyanandam, Indonesia; likewise people from the U.S.A., Singapore, the Gulf, Malaysia, the U.K. and France—in this manner, 19 people are conducting industries in Tamil Nadu with a total value of nearly Rs. 50 crore. We have no allergy to N.R.I.s. It is only when contradictions arise in the way they operate and situations develop that are harmful to our Government, our country or our people, and when such corruption is concealed—
that we are compelled to bring it out and identify it; there is no other reason, I wish to state.

Closed mills were discussed. Our Ramani spoke about them in detail this morning. In accordance with the election-time announcement that the Government would engage in efforts to reopen closed mills: Tamil Nadu Spinning Mills, Avinashi, was reopened on 10-3-1989; Vasudeva Textiles, Coimbatore, on 13-3-1989; R.A.V. Textiles, Coimbatore, on 12-4-1989; Balaji Cotton Mills, Salem, on 21-8-1989; Rukmani Mills, Silaiman, on 7-8-1989; Sarkuna Textiles, Coimbatore, on 10-7-1989; Balaji Spinners, Coimbatore, on 25-11-1989; Amaravathi Dyeing and Cotton Mills on 8-11-1989; and Deivasigamani Spinning Mills on 1-1-1990. Thus nine closed mills have been reopened.

Six mills are in a stage where reopening is proposed and negotiations are under way with the Central Government. Seven mills have been left out because they are very small and would not be viable if taken over and run. Eight mills remain under study without any decision yet. Since the Government announced its decision to take over and run certain mills itself and wrote to the Central Government but has so far received no proper reply, and because Minister Yadav, who recently came here, gave an assurance that he would look into it, our Ministers are going to Delhi. Our Handlooms Minister and Labour Welfare Minister will meet Central Ministers in Delhi and return with a good decision in another day or two. I am very happy to inform the House that these six mills will be reopened very soon. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

When Ponnusamy spoke about Neyveli royalty, in a mood that something had to be criticised and that he could not speak otherwise, he asked: what is this Rs. 2½, could you not have obtained Rs. 5? A schedule has been prepared for Neyveli coal royalty, specifying how many rupees are payable for each type of coal. According to that schedule, Neyveli coal is lignite, a somewhat lower-grade coal; therefore the schedule fixes its royalty at Rs. 2½.

But what happened was this. Vasant Sathe, Central Minister in the previous Government, wrote to me on September 26, 1989, stating that henceforth royalty would be paid at Rs. 2½ per tonne and that, from 1976 onward, a grant amount equivalent to it would be provided. He said it would be given from 1976. We said no. From 1956 to 1976, the Congress Government then in office had asked for a share in the profits. But no profit was shown there, and so no share was received. Those who showed accounts saying there had been no profit up to 1976 then, once profit began after 1976, said that the agreement for a share in profits had ended—like the Cauvery problem—that agreement had ended, and henceforth only royalty would be paid. We asked what that calculation was. In the intervening period nobody pressed the matter. After this Government came to office, it began pressing the claim. We began asking during Rajiv Gandhi's time. The reply given to us then was that, for 1976 to 1989, the grant equivalent to the royalty due was Rs. 19.09 crore, and that Rs. 7.09 crore should be deducted for electricity supplied by Neyveli Lignite Corporation to the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board—that is, for electricity supplied to the Electricity Board—leaving a net amount payable to us of Rs. 12 crore—

and they stated firmly that it was only Rs. 12 crore. After that we argued with them. Recently, talks were held at officials' level in Delhi, and they agreed to pay Rs. 4.28 crore as the royalty amount for 1956 to 1976 and, adding Rs. 19 crore as royalty from 1976 to 1986, said they would pay a total of Rs. 23.37 crore. Deducting the Rs. 7.09 crore payable by us, they said they would give Rs. 16.28 crore.

Only after that did this old man go to Delhi, meet our Minister Arif Mohammad, argue with him for a long time, and obtain Rs. 30 crore. (Sound of desk-thumping.) We said: waive that Rs. 7 crore yourselves; include that Rs. 7 crore; and on the Rs. 23 crore—besides that, pay interest for not having paid it all these years. They included the interest and we have today received Rs. 30 crore. Ponnusamy should at least have been happy about that. Instead of being happy, he asked why we had not obtained still more. That is good. It is good to ask like that. When we go there, I can say: they are asking all this here; so please give it, otherwise it is your Government that will get a bad name. I wish only to say that I will certainly make use of the Opposition speaking forcefully here when I ask them there.

Yesterday our friend Chokkar, while speaking, referred to TIIC and pointed to a discrepancy between amounts sanctioned and amounts disbursed. This is not even for a full year; it is for nine months. He read a footnote there—

and made that observation. Last year the amount sanctioned by TIIC was Rs. 103.97 crore and the amount disbursed was Rs. 60.78 crore. That is what should be noted. Rs. 103 crore was sanctioned and Rs. 60 crore was disbursed. They have now informed us that, when sanction is stated at a high figure but disbursement is low, sanctions too should be made in a measured way. After they said that, this year the amount sanctioned is Rs. 97.10 crore and the amount disbursed Rs. 65.07 crore. If one considers only the amount disbursed, it was a little over Rs. 60 crore last year and a little over Rs. 65 crore this year, so disbursement has actually increased. We have accepted their view and, on the basis of what IDBI said when giving its opinion, we have sanctioned and disbursed in this manner; there is no other reason.

They said one more thing, using a good example: “Old wine in new bottle or different bottles.” At a time when cheap liquor is being discussed, they spoke about wine. They said that sales-tax deferral and Interest free Sales Tax Loan are both the same thing, and therefore the same wine is being poured into two bottles. But that is not the truth. Under the interest-free sales-tax loan scheme, the sales tax is first paid properly and then, subject to a ceiling, an equivalent interest-free loan is given by Government industrial-development institutions; that is the sales-tax loan scheme. Because there can sometimes be a time gap between paying the sales tax and receiving the interest-free loan, causing delay and creating the possibility of financial strain for the undertaking, this Government fully implemented the sales-tax deferral scheme to avoid that problem.

Deferring sales tax is one scheme. The sales-tax loan scheme is one thing; the sales-tax deferral scheme is another. The two are not the same. To implement this properly, authority to grant it has been given at district level to the Assistant Commissioner, Commercial Taxes. We are also going to bring in a legal amendment to implement it. Thus arrangements will be made for the sales-tax deferral scheme to operate promptly and quickly at district level.

Even so, for industries that have been receiving loans for one or two years under the earlier sales-tax loan scheme to continue obtaining such loans, we have allotted Rs. 10.5 crore in the Budget. They may, if they wish, opt to shift themselves to the sales-tax deferral scheme, or they may continue to obtain loans under the sales-tax loan scheme. Provision has therefore been made for both schemes. Continuing from this, I wish to announce a few more matters to the House.

Yesterday Chokkar searched. He said, “I am searching, searching and still searching; I cannot find it.” They had announced all these sales-tax concessions and said that, out of 105 taluks, 30 would be classified as most backward; he asked where he was to look for them. I waited, thinking, let him search, let him search for a whole day. Sometimes even when announcements are made here today, they appear incorrectly in newspapers; therefore I have had these announcements printed, and they will be distributed later.
For these 105 areas already declared, through our Tamil Nadu Industrial Investment Corporation—“TIIC”—we have provided Rs. 6 crore, and through SIPCOT Rs. 2.74 crore—

and through the Directorate of Industries and Commerce Rs. 56 lakh, making a total of Rs. 9.30 crore. But among the 105 areas declared backward, only 44 taluks in 17 districts have used this subsidy to establish industries. Here 323 medium and large industries have been started. Among the 105 areas, in only 44 taluks in 17 districts, 323 medium and large industries have been started. Since it would be useful to state them even if time is short, and since this concerns industrial subsidy, I wish to list them.

In Chengai-Anna district: Cheyyur 1. Kanchipuram, benefited industry 1. Madurantakam 27, Ponneri 22, Tiruttani 1, Gummidipoondi 15—this does not come within the 105. In Chidambaranar district, Vilathikulam 2; Coimbatore, Pollachi 2, Avinashi 18; Dharmapuri, Denkanikottai 4, Dharmapuri 7, Harur 4, Krishnagiri 2, Pennagaram 1; Dindigul Quaid-e-Millath district, Palani 28, Vadipatti 3, Vedasandur 3; Kanyakumari, Thovalai 3; Madurai, Andipatti 5, Periyakulam 4; Tirunelveli-Kattabomman, Nanguneri 7, Radhapuram 4, Tenkasi 1; in the Nilgiris, some industries at Gudalur. That is all. North Arcot-Ambedkar district: Cheyyar 4, Polur 1; Pasumpon Thevar Thirumaganar, Karaikudi 2, Sivaganga 1, Dharapuram 7, Gobichettipalayam 2, Perundurai 6. Pudukkottai district: Alangudi 3, 1, Aranthangi 4, Avudaiyarkoil 6, Gandarvakottai, Tirumayam 3; Ramanathapuram district, Ramanathapuram 2; Salem, Attur 1, Sankagiri 1; South Arcot district, Chidambaram 8, Gingee 1, Kallakurichi 15, Kattumannarkoil 3, Tindivanam 10, Ulundurpet 7, Villupuram 1; Tiruchirappalli, Musiri 64, Perambalur 5. Thus 323 industries have benefited. Only in 44 taluks out of the 105 have they received this assistance and started industries. That is why, within the 105, we are dividing them into “backward” and “most backward,” and thirty taluks—
are being separately identified so that some additional concessions may be given to them. I wish now to announce that effort of the Government.

If you ask how we determine a backward area and a most-backward area: for a backward area, the average proportion of industrial workers must be below the State average of 1.26 per cent. In the same taluk, the value of large or medium industries must be below Rs. 15 crore. We include such areas under B.C.—backward areas. On this basis, we have taken 105 areas.

Then, how do we determine M.B.C.? The average proportion of factory workers in that taluk must be below 25 per cent. There must be no medium industry or any large industry in that taluk. On that basis, thirty backward taluks have been selected.

I wish to read their names here. In Chengai-Anna district, Pallipattu; in Dharmapuri, Pennagaram; in Dindigul Quaid-e-Millath district, Vedasandur and Kodaikanal; in Kamarajar district, Tiruchuli; in Madurai, Usilampatti; in Tirunelveli-Kattabomman district, Tenkasi and Radhapuram; in Periyar district, Gobichettipalayam; in Salem district, Yercaud; in South Arcot district, Kattumannarkoil and Tirukovilur. Nobody should be jealous of Thanjavur district—it is a district where there is no industry. In Thanjavur district: Papanasam, Valangaiman, Kudavasal, Peravurani, Nannilam, Orathanadu, Sirkazhi, Pattukkottai, Tiruvarur and Tiruthuraipoondi. (Laughter, interruption.) If the pipeline he asked for comes, industries will come there too.

In Tiruchirappalli district: Udayarpalayam and Thuraiyur; in North Arcot-Ambedkar district: Arcot; in Tiruvannamalai-Sambuvarayar district: Chengam, Polur, Cheyyar and Vandavasi; in Pudukkottai district: Avudaiyarkoil. Apart from these, I wish to place a few more announcements before you.

With the objective that Tamil Nadu should implement an incentive-concession scheme of the finest kind in India, I have come forward to offer further concessions. In the SIPCOT industrial complexes at Gudalur, Pudukkottai and Manamadurai and in the thirty taluks mentioned above, industries that are started will receive sales-tax exemption as stated earlier—that is, sales-tax exemption for five years. In the remaining seventy-five backward taluks and in industrial centres run by Government undertakings, the sales-tax deferral scheme for industries started there will be completely restructured. (Sound of desk-thumping.) The sales-tax deferral scheme is being restructured for expansion of industries (Part 1) and for establishment of new industries (Part 2).

At present, under both these schemes, the ceiling for sales-tax deferral is Rs. 3 crore. For newly started industries, that ceiling of Rs. 3 crore will hereafter be relaxed and raised up to the amount of capital expenditure. For industries undertaking expansion, it will be provided up to 80 per cent of capital expenditure. Under both parts of the scheme, sales-tax deferral will be available for up to nine years. I announce this here after considering the way industries are attracted to Maharashtra and Gujarat because of such concessions.
After nine years, these industrial undertakings need only begin paying sales tax. After nine years, they must pay the sales tax for that year together with the sales tax deferred for the first year—

At present, in other areas of Tamil Nadu, apart from pioneer industries, there has so far been no sales-tax deferral scheme for other industries. Hereafter, the sales-tax deferral scheme will be extended to all industries in the other areas as well. In those areas, the scheme will apply both to expansion of industries (Part 1) and to new industries (Part 2). New industries will receive sales-tax deferral for five years, with a ceiling of 60 per cent of capital expenditure. For expansion of existing industries, the ceiling will be 50 per cent of capital expenditure.

Further, with the good intention that large industries should be started in the State, industries commenced with capital expenditure above Rs. 50 crore will, as a special concession, receive sales-tax deferral for nine years up to the amount of capital expenditure, no matter in which part of the State they are established. (Sound of desk-thumping.) I believe this announcement will create a good opportunity for large industries to arise in the State.

Therefore, though there is not enough time to answer and explain every one of the many views you have given, I will keep them all in my heart and take the necessary action. Let us all join together and develop industry in Tamil Nadu. With that appeal, and requesting that the cut motions be withdrawn, I take my seat.
